1.note: Paul names himself as the writer of this letter to the believers in the church at Ephesus (and elsewhere). Except where noted, all instances of “you” and “your” refer to the Ephesian believers as well as to all believers, and so are plural.

1.q: Παῦλος, ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ & τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν
1.note: Your language may have a particular way of introducing the author of a letter and the intended audience. Alternate translation: [I, Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ … write this letter to you, God’s holy people]

The phrase **in Christ Jesus** and similar expressions are metaphors that frequently occur in the New Testament letters. They express the strongest kind of relationship possible between Christ and those who believe in him, picturing believers as being surrounded by Christ. Alternate translation: [in close relationship to Christ Jesus]

2.note: This is a common greeting and blessing that Paul often uses in the beginning of his letters. Use a form in your language that makes it clear that this is a greeting and blessing.

3.note: In this book, unless otherwise stated, the words “us” and “we” refer to Paul, the believers in Ephesus, and all believers.

This verse provides background information about the Ephesians to help readers understand their spiritual condition. Paul opens his letter by talking about the believers’ position and their safety before God.

3.q: εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
3.note: If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. Alternate translation: [Let us praise the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ]
Alternate translation: [for God has blessed us]
Alternate translation: [every blessing coming from the Spirit of God]

Paul assumes that his readers will understand that the word **heavenly** refers to the place where God is. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the supernatural world]

Here, **in Christ** could mean: (1) a metaphor referring to our close relationship with Christ. Alternate translation: [by uniting us with Christ] or [because we are united with Christ]; (2) what Christ has done. Alternate translation: [through Christ] or [through what Christ has done]

4.note: Paul uses the two similar words **holy** and **blameless** to emphasize moral goodness. If your language does not have two similar words, you can use one word for both, as in the UST.

The word **blameless** contains two negative ideas: “blame” or “fault,” and “-less,” which means “without.” If it would be helpful in your language, the two negative ideas can be replaced with the corresponding positive idea, “perfect.”

5.note: The words “he,” “himself,” and “his” refer to God.
The word **us** refers to Paul, the Ephesian church, and all believers in Christ. Alternate translation: [God planned long ago to adopt us]
Alternate translation: [God chose us ahead of time] or [God chose us long ago]
Here, **adoption** is a metaphor that refers to becoming part of God’s family. Alternate translation: [to become his children]
Paul assumes that his readers will understand that God brought believers into his family by the work of **Jesus Christ**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

6.note: Alternate translation: [he has kindly given to us by means of the One whom he loves]
Alternate translation: [the One he loves, Jesus Christ] or [his Son, whom he loves]

7.note: The **blood** of Jesus is a metonym for his death. Alternate translation: [because he died]
Paul speaks of God’s **grace** as if it were material wealth. Alternate translation: [greatness of God’s grace] or [abundance of God’s grace]

8.note: Alternate translation: [which he gave us in a great amount] or [being extremely kind to us]
This could mean: (1) because he has all wisdom and understanding. (2) so that we might have great wisdom and understanding.
Here, **wisdom** and **understanding** mean very similar things. If your language does not have two similar words, you can use one word for both.

9.note: This could mean: (1) because he wanted to make it known to us. (2) which was what he wanted.
Alternate translation: [as he demonstrated this purpose in Christ]

10.note: A new sentence could be started here. Alternate translation: [He did this with a view to an administration] or [He did this, thinking about a stewardship]
Alternate translation: [when the time is right] or [at the time that he has appointed]
Alternate translation: [under his rule] or [under his authority]

11.note: Both pronouns **we** and **We** are inclusive in this verse. Paul is referring to all Christians, who were predestined to belong to Christ. In verses 12 and 13 he will divide this group into “we” (exclusive) Jewish Christians and “you” Gentile Christians.
If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. This could mean: (1) God also chose us to be his possession. (2) God also chose us to be heirs.
If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. Alternate translation: [God chose us ahead of time] or [God chose us long ago]

12.q: ἡμᾶς & τοὺς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ
12.note: Here, the word **we** is exclusive and refers to the Jewish believers who first heard the good news, not the believers at Ephesus.

12.q: εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς, εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης αὐτοῦ
12.note: Alternate translation: [so that we … would live to praise him for his glory]

13.note: Paul has been speaking in the previous two verses about himself and the other Jewish believers, but now he begins speaking about the Ephesian believers.
This could mean: (1) the message about the truth. (2) the true message.

13.q: ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ Πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, τῷ Ἁγίῳ
13.note: In this metaphor Paul pictures the **Holy Spirit** as a seal, comparing him to the wax that was placed on a letter and stamped with a symbol representing the person who wrote the letter. Paul uses this custom as a picture to show how God has used the Holy Spirit to assure us that we belong to him. Alternate translation: [God has placed the Holy Spirit that he promised on you as if he were a seal]
If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. Alternate translation: [God has sealed you]

14.note: Receiving that which God has promised is spoken of in terms of one inheriting property or wealth from a family member. Alternate translation: [an initial portion that we will receive from what God has promised] or [a guarantee that we will receive what God has promised to give us]

15.note: The connecting phrase **Because of this** introduces a reason-result relationship. The reason is that the Ephesians had believed the gospel and had been sealed by the Holy Spirit. The result is that Paul praises God. Use a phrase in your language that connects a reason to a result.

16.note: Paul is using a figure of speech here that expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the positive meaning. Paul uses **not stopped** to emphasize that he continues to thank God. Alternate translation: [I continue to thank God]
Paul uses this exaggeration to emphasize that he thanks God very often. Alternate translation: [I continue to thank God] or [I often thank God]

17.note: The connecting phrase **so that** introduces a reason-result relationship. The reason is that Paul prays for the Ephesians. The result is that God would enlighten the Ephesians about all that he has done for them through Christ. Use a phrase in your language that connects a reason to a result.

17.q: πνεῦμα σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως, ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ
17.note: Alternate translation: [spiritual wisdom to understand his revelation]

18.note: Here, **heart** refers to a person’s mind or thinking. Alternate translation: [that you may gain understanding]
If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. Alternate translation: [that God may give you understanding] or [that God may enlighten your mind]
The phrase **eyes of your heart** is a metaphor for one’s ability to gain understanding. Alternate translation: [that you may gain understanding and be enlightened]
Alternate translation: [may be made to see]

Paul assumes that his readers will understand that the **calling** of God refers to his choosing people to believe in him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that you have because he chose you to be his people]
Receiving what God has promised to believers is spoken of as if one were inheriting property and wealth from a family member.
Alternate translation: [those whom he has set apart for himself] or [those who belong completely to him]

19.q: τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ
19.note: Alternate translation: [God’s power, which is far beyond all other power]

19.q: τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ
19.note: Alternate translation: [his great power that is at work for us]
The words **force** and **strength** have very similar meanings and may be combined. Alternate translation: [of his great strength]

20.note: Alternate translation: [when he made him alive again]
This expression describes all **dead** people together in the underworld. To come back from among them speaks of becoming alive again. Alternate translation: [from among all those who have died]

20.q: καθίσας ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ, ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις
20.note: The one who sits at the **right hand** of a king sits at his right side and rules with all the authority of the king at whose right hand or side he sits. This is a metonym of location that represents the authority that the person in that location possesses. Alternate translation: [gave him all authority to rule from heaven]
To sit at the **right hand** of God is a symbolic action meaning “receiving great honor and authority from God.” Alternate translation: [seated him in the place of honor and authority beside him]
The word **heavenly** refers to the place where God is. See how you translated this in Ephesians 1:3.

21.q: ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς, καὶ ἐξουσίας, καὶ δυνάμεως, καὶ κυριότητος
21.note: These are all terms for the ranks of supernatural beings, both angelic and demonic. If your language does not have four different terms for rulers or authorities, you can combine them. Alternate translation: [far above all types of supernatural beings]
If your language does not use this passive form, you can state this in active form. This could mean: (1) every name that man gives. (2) every name that God gives.
Here, **name** could refer to: (1) a title. (2) a position of authority.

22.note: Here, **feet** represents Christ’s lordship, authority, and power. Alternate translation: [under Christ’s power]
Here, **head** is a metaphor that refers to the leader or the one who is in charge. Alternate translation: [ruler over all things]

23.note: Just as the head (verse 22) rules all things pertaining to a human body, so Christ is the head of the church **body**.

23.q: τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν πληρουμένου
23.note: Alternate translation: [for Christ fills the church with his life and power just as he gives life to all things]
This could have: (1) a passive sense, which would mean that Christ fills or completes the church. (2) an active sense, which would mean that the church completes Christ (as a body completes a head).
